title: A changing appointment service
scenario: A clinic needs an appointment portal. Staff disagree about booking rules, a working version is needed soon, and requirements are likely to change after use. Management proposes freezing all requirements now and delivering everything at once.
prompts: Identify why the proposed process creates rework risk.
Recommend a process model and explain how it accommodates change.
Choose two agile/XP (Extreme Programming) practices and explain the role of customer feedback.
modelSolution: An early freeze is risky because the workflow is not yet agreed. Prototype the disputed booking flow to anticipate change, then use incremental development and delivery to tolerate later changes. Review small usable increments with clinic staff. Test-first development protects booking rules as they change; continuous integration and refactoring keep changes manageable. Explain constraints rather than claiming agile eliminates rework.
rubric: Connects two practices to the scenario

title: From vague requests to testable requirements
scenario: Patients request “easy booking”; receptionists request “no conflicting appointments”; management requests “instant responses.” The portal must use the organization’s existing identity service. The first draft combines these requests into one sentence.
prompts: Classify services and constraints, distinguishing abstraction from requirement type.
Describe elicitation with the stakeholder groups and resolve ambiguity.
Write a structured booking requirement and identify validation checks and a test.
modelSolution: Booking and preventing conflicts are functional behavior; a negotiated response-time limit is a product non-functional constraint, and mandatory use of an organizational service is an organizational constraint. User versus system requirements is a separate abstraction dimension. Interview the groups with examples, expose disagreements, and validate a prototype. Split requirements, assign stable IDs (identifiers), record rationale/source, inputs, function, outputs, dependencies, and tests. Agree measurable response conditions rather than inventing a threshold. Check validity, consistency, completeness, realism, and verifiability; test a conflicting booking with specified input and expected rejection.
rubric: Uses structured fields and stable IDs (identifiers)
Explains validation and a repeatable test

title: Choose a boundary, then model user goals
scenario: An appointment portal lets a patient book an appointment and cancel it. Booking always checks availability. A separate identity service authenticates users; a separate notification service delivers confirmations. The portal is the system under design.
prompts: Explain the context boundary and external relationships.
Identify actors and user-goal use cases for the portal.
Explain the include relationship and how a context model differs from a use-case diagram.
modelSolution: Place the Appointment portal inside the context boundary, with Patient, Identity service, and Notification service outside. Connect each external entity to the portal. For the scoped use-case exercise, Patient associates with Book appointment and Cancel appointment. Book appointment includes Check availability, with the arrow toward Check availability. The use cases lie inside the boundary and Patient outside. Context relationships describe the environment; use-case associations and include describe interactions/goals and required reused behavior. Do not replace either with internal call sequences.
rubric: Clear system boundary and external entities
commonMistakes: Putting external services inside the portal
Treating availability checking as the patient’s standalone goal
